newsitem.title: ROMANIA: IMF backs objectives of new Romanian leaders.
newsitem.headline: IMF backs objectives of new Romanian leaders.

text.p: A top International Monetary fund official on Friday said Romania had sunk into a grimmer economic crisis than previously believed, but backed the new government's broad commitment to speed up market reforms.

Poul Thomsen, the IMF's senior negotiator for Romania, said after more than a week of talks that the economy had deteriorated considerably in the final months of the ousted government run by ex-communists.

He said the programme submitted to parliament this week by its reformist successor voted in last month contained the basis for real change. But any resumption of the IMF's suspended credits, he said, required long negotiations in the New Year.
"We found the economic situation definitely quite difficult, more difficult than in June or September. Things gradually got worse," Thomsen told a news conference.
"We are very pleased with the general objectives of the government programme. But like you, we have not seen the details. We are looking forward to seeing those details."
Thomsen said the main objective of his visit was to assess the state of the economy and not to determine future strategy.
He held talks with Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea for the second time on Friday a day after his government took office.
He also met President Emil Constantinescu, who last month defeated Ion Iliescu, the former communist who had run Romania since the 1989 execution of dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.

IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus visits Romania next week and negotiators begin talks in January on a new standby credit. The previous three-year credit of $460 million was suspended this year with the IMF criticising foreign exchange market restrictions and overspending.

Thomsen said the budget deficit had soared to five percent of gross domestic product against the IMF-backed objective of 2.2 percent. Central Bank chairman Mugur Isarescu told reporters inflation this year would climb to 38 to 45 percent against a 20 percent target.
Ciorbea's programme, overwhelmingly approved by parliament, contained few concrete figures.

It set as objectives faster privatisation, restructuring of industry and farming, tax cuts, increased social benefits and a clampdown on corruption. The prime minister said he wanted annual growth of 4.5 to six percent.
Thomsen told Reuters ministers were right to seek reduced subsidies to farming and energy-intensive industries.
"It is in these two sectors that system deficits have again and again brought down stabilisation programmes," he said.
"This is what we need to make stabilisation programmes sustainable. As far as how to quantify the programme for the next year, we have not entered into that discussion."
